common_name: Early Snowball Cauliflower (Classic Compact Heirloom White Cauliflower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or sow in mid-summer for fall harvest; Early Snowball has been a mainstay of American seed catalogs since the late 1800s and remains one of the fastest, most reliable open-pollinated cauliflowers for gardeners in short-season climates.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant sturdy seedlings into rich, evenly moist soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants 15-20 inches apart; Early Snowball is a compact, open-pollinated heirloom that has stayed popular for well over a century because it forms tight, pure-white 5-6 inch heads faster and more dependably than many modern hybrids. Tie the outer leaves loosely over the developing curd once it reaches golf-ball size to shield it from sun and keep the head bright white, checking every few days since this variety heads up quickly once it starts. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from healthy plants that are isolated from other Brassica oleracea varieties in bloom. Harvest as soon as heads reach full size and are still tight and smooth, since Early Snowball's curds loosen and turn ricey faster than slower-maturing types if left too long in the field.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company historical seed catalogs

common_name: Giant of Naples Celery (Sedano Gigante di Napoli, Italian Heirloom Braising Celery)
scientific_name: Apium graveolens var. dulce 'Giant of Naples'

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since the seed germinates slowly and seedlings need a long head start before it is warm enough to transplant; Giant of Naples is a traditional southern Italian heirloom grown for its thick, tender, mild ribs prized for braising and slow-cooked dishes.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil that stays consistently moist, since celery's shallow roots suffer quickly in dry spells and stress produces tough, stringy, bitter stalks. Giant of Naples is a classic heirloom from the Campania region of Italy, grown less often as a raw salad celery and more as a cooking celery, since its thick, pale-green ribs soften into a rich, mellow flavor that anchors soffritto, braises, and long-simmered sauces. The stalks are notably broad and fleshy compared to standard American celery, and the plant tends to be more heat-tolerant and less prone to bolting than delicate salad types. Harvest by cutting individual outer stalks as needed through the season, or dig the whole plant once it reaches full size; a light frost sweetens the flavor rather than damaging the crop.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Celery Production

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date once the soil has warmed slightly; Kabuli is the large, cream-colored, thin-skinned chickpea market class familiar from grocery-store dried and canned garbanzo beans, distinct from the smaller, darker Desi types grown mainly in South Asia.

directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep into well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH, since chickpeas rot quickly in cold, wet ground and dislike heavy clay. Kabuli chickpeas produce the large, plump, beige-cream seeds most familiar to home cooks as garbanzo beans or hummus chickpeas, borne one or two per small, inflated pod on bushy, ferny-leaved plants that rarely need staking. The foliage and pods are covered in fine glandular hairs that exude a sticky, mildly acidic secretion, so wear long sleeves and gloves when working among mature plants to avoid skin irritation. Pick pods green and shell them for fresh eating like a shelling pea, or let the crop dry down fully in the field and harvest whole plants once most pods have turned tan and papery, then thresh, winnow, and store the dried seed in a sealed container.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Cicer arietinum germplasm resources
Washington State University Extension — Dry Pea and Chickpea Production

common_name: Black Kabuli Chickpea (Dark-Seeded Heirloom Garbanzo Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date; Black Kabuli is an heirloom chickpea combining the larger seed size of Kabuli types with a dark, near-black seed coat, valued by gardeners for its rich, nutty flavor and striking appearance in salads and stews.

directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep in well-drained soil once the danger of hard frost has passed, giving plants full sun and lean-to-average fertility, since overly rich soil favors foliage over pod set. Black Kabuli produces the same bushy, drought-tolerant growth habit as other chickpeas, but each pod holds one or two dark brown to near-black seeds that keep their striking color when dried, making them a favorite for gardeners who like to grow and cook heirloom bean and legume varieties not found in stores. Flavor is often described as earthier and nuttier than standard tan Kabuli chickpeas, and the dried seeds hold their shape well in long-simmered stews. Handle mature plants carefully, since the foliage and pods carry the same sticky, irritating hairs typical of the species; harvest once most pods have dried and turned brittle, then thresh and store the seed somewhere cool and dry.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Cicer arietinum germplasm resources

common_name: Jaune Paille des Vertus Shallot (Classic French Golden Storage Shallot)
scientific_name: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Jaune Paille des Vertus'

planting.note: Plant bulb sets 4-8 weeks before last frost in spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones 7-10; Jaune Paille des Vertus is a nineteenth-century French heirloom named for the village of Vertus in the Champagne region and prized above all for its exceptionally long storage life.

directions: Plant individual bulb sets pointed-end-up, about 1 inch deep and 6-8 inches apart, in fertile, well-drained soil, and keep the bed evenly moist through the growing season while easing off water as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over. Jaune Paille des Vertus, whose name translates roughly as "golden straw of Vertus," is one of the oldest documented French shallot varieties still in commerce, each set multiplying into a tight cluster of coppery-gold, papery-skinned bulbs with pale yellow flesh and the classic mild, sweet-sharp shallot flavor. It has long been regarded by French market gardeners as the standard keeping shallot, holding firm in storage for many months longer than most modern shallot varieties when properly cured. Harvest once the tops have fully collapsed and dried, cure the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded spot for two to three weeks, and store the cleaned bulbs somewhere cool, dry, and dark.
sources: Kokopelli Seed Foundation (French heirloom vegetable archive)
